name: 3 Maccabees
sourceNote: Translated fresh from the Greek text of 3 Maccabees in H. B. Swete's edition of the Septuagint (Cambridge, 1909; public domain), with Brenton's public-domain English version consulted as a check. Despite its title, the book has nothing to do with the Maccabean revolt: written in Greek, probably in Alexandria in the first century BC, it tells how the Jews of Egypt were persecuted under Ptolemy IV Philopator (221–204 BC) and miraculously delivered. Its style is ornate and its Greek is sometimes obscure; such places are noted. Dates by Egyptian months are given in the text with the modern month span, and the original reckoning is in a footnote. Weights and sums of money are given in approximate modern US units, with the original units and metric figures in the footnotes. Greek kyrios is translated "Lord" and theos "God." Verse numbers follow the standard English versification. This is a draft awaiting scholarly review.

verses.text: Philopator,{a} learning from those who had come back of the taking away by Antiochus{b} of the places held under him, sent word to all his forces, infantry and cavalry, and taking along his sister Arsinoe{c} he marched out as far as the districts near Raphia, where Antiochus's side had pitched camp.{d}

But a certain Theodotus, intending to carry out a plot, took with him the best of the Ptolemaic weapons that had earlier been put under his command and crossed over by night to Ptolemy's tent, as if alone to kill him and in this way to dissolve the war.

But Dositheus, called the son of Drimylus, a Jew by race who later changed his customs and became estranged from the ancestral teachings, had led the king away and laid some insignificant man down in the tent; and it fell to this man to receive the punishment meant for the other.

A fierce battle took place, and matters were going more strongly for Antiochus; then Arsinoe went up and down the forces many times, and with lament and tears, her locks let loose, she called on them to help themselves and their children and wives boldly, promising to give each of them, if they won, two and a half pounds of gold.{e}
And so it happened that the opponents were destroyed in hand-to-hand combat, and many also were taken captive by the spear.
Having prevailed over the plot, he decided to go to the neighboring cities and encourage them.
By doing this, and by allotting gifts to the sacred precincts, he made those under him of good courage.

When the Jews sent to him some from the council of elders{f} and from the elders to greet him, to bring guest-gifts, and to rejoice with him over what had happened, it came about that he was the more eager to visit them as soon as possible.

Having crossed over to Jerusalem, he sacrificed to the faithful God and rendered thanks, and did something of what was fitting for the place. And indeed on coming into the place, he was struck by its earnestness and decorum,
and marveling also at the good order of the temple, he took it into his mind to plan to enter the shrine.

When they said that this was not fitting, because not even the members of the nation were permitted to enter, nor even all the priests, but only the high priest, who presides over all, and he only once a year,{g} he was in no way persuaded.
Even when the law was read out to him, he did not leave off putting himself forward, saying that he must go in: "Even if those men are deprived of this honor, I ought not to be."
And he inquired for what reason, when he entered every sacred precinct, no one of those present had stopped him.
And someone thoughtlessly said that he was wrong to make a marvel of this very thing.{h}
"But since this has happened," he said, "why should I not enter in any case, whether they wish it or not?"

Then the priests in all their vestments prostrated themselves and begged the greatest God to help in the present plight and to turn aside the onset of the one who was wickedly attacking; and they filled the temple with cries and tears.
Those who had remained behind in the city were alarmed and rushed out, taking it that something mysterious was happening.
And the maidens shut away in their rooms burst out along with those who bore them; they strewed their tresses with dust and crammed the broad ways with wailing and moans.
Those who had lately been dressed for marriage{i} left the bridal chambers arranged for meeting and the modesty that becomes them, and ran about in disorder through the city.
Mothers and nurses who had charge of the infants left them, one this way and one that, some in the houses and some along the lanes, and without turning back they thronged to the all-highest temple.
Many-sided was the supplication of those who had gathered there because of what was being unholily attempted by him.
With them the bolder of the citizens would not endure his pressing on and intending to fulfill his purpose;

calling out to make a rush for arms and to die boldly for the ancestral law, they caused much roughness in the place; and being turned back with difficulty by the aged and the elders, they joined in the same stance of supplication.
Meanwhile the throng, as before, kept on in prayer.
The elders around the king tried in many ways to divert his arrogant mind from the plot he had conceived.
But he grew bold and dismissed them all, and was already making his approach, thinking he would bring the aforesaid deed to completion.

Those around him, seeing these things, turned as well, joining with our people in calling on the One holding all might to defend them in what was at hand, not overlooking the lawless and arrogant deed.
From the dense and laboring cry of the crowds as they gathered rose an indescribable shout;
It seemed as if not only the human beings but even the walls and the entire ground were resounding, since everyone then was ready to exchange life for death rather than see the place made profane.

notes.text: Ptolemy IV Philopator, king of Egypt 221–204 BC. "Philopator" means "father-loving."
Antiochus III the Great, king of the Seleucid empire 223–187 BC.
Arsinoe III, sister and wife of Ptolemy IV.
Raphia, on the coast southwest of Gaza; the battle was fought in 217 BC, and Ptolemy won.
Greek "two minas of gold"; a mina was about 1.25 lb (570 g).
Greek gerousia, the senate or council of elders.
Or "that it was wrong to boast of this very thing"; the Greek is obscure.
The Greek of this verse is obscure; the translation is approximate.

verses.text: Then the high priest Simon, facing the shrine, bent his knees, stretched out his hands in seemly order, and made a supplication of this kind:{a}

"Lord, Lord, King of the heavens and Master of all creation, holy among the holy ones, sole ruler, Almighty, give heed to us who are worn down by an unholy and profane man, swollen with insolence and strength.
For you are the one who created all things, and you hold sway over the universe; you are a righteous potentate, and you judge those who do anything in outrage and haughtiness.
You destroyed those who did wrong before, among whom were giants trusting in might and boldness, bringing upon them water beyond measure.{b}
You burned up with fire and sulfur the Sodomites, workers of arrogance, who had become notorious for their vices, and you set them as a pattern for those coming after.{c}
You put the bold Pharaoh to the proof, he who had enslaved your holy people Israel, with many and varied punishments, and made your power known, by which you made known your great might.

Him, as he gave chase with chariots and a horde of soldiery, you flooded over with the sea's deep; yet those who had put their trust in you, the ruler of the whole creation, you carried across unharmed.
These, beholding what your hand had wrought, sang the praise of you, the All-powerful.

You, O King, when you created the boundless and immeasurable earth, chose this city and hallowed this place for your name, though you have need of nothing; and you glorified it with a magnificent manifestation, establishing it for the glory of your great and honored name.
And loving the house of Israel, you promised that if we should fall away and distress should overtake us, and we should come to this place and pray, you would hear our prayer.{d}
And indeed you are faithful and true.
For many a time, when our forefathers were hard pressed, you came to their aid in their low estate and delivered them out of grievous ills.
see now, holy King, because of our many and great sins we are worn down, made subject to our enemies, and slack in our weakness.
And in our downfall this bold and profane man is bent on outraging the holy place set apart on earth for the name of your glory.
For your dwelling, the heaven of heaven, is unreachable by human beings.
But since you were pleased to place your glory among your people Israel, you hallowed this place.
Do not take vengeance on us for the uncleanness of these men, nor call us to account for their profanation, lest the lawless boast in their rage and exult in the arrogance of their tongue, saying,
'The sanctified house we have trodden underfoot, just as the shrines of the loathsome idols are trodden.'
Wipe away our sins, scatter our errors, and make your mercy shine forth at this hour.
Let your compassions overtake us quickly, and put praises in the mouths of those who are fallen and crushed in soul, making peace for us."
Thereupon God, who oversees all, the first Father, holy among the holy ones, having heard the lawful entreaty, scourged him who was greatly lifted up in insolence and boldness;
he shook him this way and that like a reed by the wind, so that he lay on the ground powerless, paralyzed in his limbs, unable even to speak, struck by a just judgment.
Then both Friends and bodyguards, seeing the swift punishment that had overtaken him, and fearing that he might even lose his life, quickly dragged him out, stricken with overwhelming fear.
Some time later, when he had recovered himself, he in no way came to repentance for having been rebuked, but departed uttering bitter threats.
When he had crossed over to Egypt, he increased his wickedness through the drinking companions and comrades already mentioned, men estranged from all justice.{e}

He was not content with countless licentious deeds, but even went on to such a pitch of boldness that he framed slanders in those places, and many of his Friends, fixing their gaze on the king's purpose, themselves followed his will.
He proposed to inflict public disgrace upon the nation: on the tower beside the court he set up a pillar and carved an inscription:

"None who do not sacrifice shall enter their sanctuaries; and all the Jews shall be brought to a registration and the condition of slaves; those who speak against it shall be taken by force and removed from life.
Those who are registered shall be branded by fire on their bodies with the ivy leaf, the emblem of Dionysus, and shall be enrolled according to their former restricted status."{f}
But in order not to appear hateful to all, he wrote beneath: "But if any of them choose to live among those initiated into the mysteries, these shall have equal citizenship with the Alexandrians."
Now some, superficially loathing the steps to be climbed toward the city's piety,{g} readily gave themselves up, as if they would share in some great fame from the association to come with the king.
But the greater part held firm with a noble soul and did not depart from their piety; offering their goods in exchange for life, they fearlessly attempted to save themselves from the registrations.
They were in good hope of obtaining help, and they abhorred those who parted from them, judged them enemies of the nation, and deprived them of common fellowship and mutual service.

notes.text: This verse is missing from the electronic edition of Swete's text used for this translation, though it belongs to the transmitted text; it is translated here from the Greek reflected in Brenton's version. Simon II, high priest around 219–196 BC (compare Sir 50:1–21).
See Gen 6:1–7.
See Gen 19:24–25.
The Greek of vv. 25–26 is loosely constructed.
Or "enrolled in their former restricted status"; the Greek is obscure. The registration (laographia) apparently reduced the Jews to the status of tax-paying natives.
The phrase is obscure; it may mean that they were glad to abandon the hard steps of their own faith for the city's religion.

verses.text: When the impious man learned of this, he grew so furious that he was not only enraged at those in Alexandria but set himself even more harshly against those in the countryside, and ordered that all should be quickly gathered into one place and removed from life by a most cruel fate.

While this was being arranged, a hostile report was spread abroad against the race by men who agreed together to do harm, a pretext being given for the slander that the Jews were keeping others from their customs.{a}
The Jews, however, were maintaining goodwill and unswerving loyalty toward the kings;
but revering God and living by his law, they kept themselves separate in the matter of foods, and for this reason they appeared hateful to some.
Yet adorning their way of life with the good practice of righteous deeds, they had come to be well regarded by all people.
This good practice of the race, talked of everywhere, the foreigners took no account of at all;

but they kept talking of the difference in worship and foods, claiming that these people were allies neither of the king nor of his forces, but were hostile and greatly opposed to the state's affairs; and they fastened no ordinary reproach upon them.{b}

The Greeks in the city, who had in no way been wronged, seeing an unexpected tumult around these people and gatherings taking place without warning, were not strong enough to help, for the regime was tyrannical; but they gave encouragement and were distressed, and supposed that these things would change;
for so great a community, guilty of nothing, would not be thus overlooked.
And already some neighbors, friends, and business partners, drawing certain of them aside in secret, gave pledges to protect them and to put forth every effort for their help.
That man, then, puffed up by his present good fortune and not perceiving the might of the supreme God, but supposing that he would continue always in the same purpose, wrote this letter against them:
"King Ptolemy Philopator, to his commanders and troops throughout Egypt and in each locality: rejoice and be well.
I myself am in good health, and so are our affairs.
Since our campaign into Asia, of which you yourselves know, was brought to its end as planned through the unfailing alliance of the gods,
we thought it right to nurture the nations inhabiting Coele-Syria and Phoenicia{c} not by force of the spear but by forbearance and much humanity, gladly doing them good.
And after assigning revenues in great abundance to the shrines city by city, we were led on also to go up to Jerusalem, to honor the temple of those accursed men who never cease from their folly.
They welcomed our presence in word but falsely in deed; for when we were eager to enter their shrine and honor it with splendid and most beautiful offerings,
carried away by their ancient arrogance, they barred us from entering, though they fell short of our might, owing to the humanity we hold toward all people.
Making their ill will toward us evident, as the only one of the nations holding their necks high against kings and their own benefactors, they are not willing to bear anything genuine.
"But we, bearing with their folly, and having come back with victory, and on arriving in Egypt meeting all the nations with humanity, have done as was fitting.

Amid these things we made known to all our forgetfulness of wrongs toward their kinsmen, both because of the alliance and because of the countless affairs entrusted to them in sincerity from the beginning; and we wished to venture a change, to count them worthy of Alexandrian citizenship and to make them partakers in our perpetual rites.{d}
But they, taking it in the opposite sense and thrusting away the good with their inborn malice, constantly inclining toward the base,

not only rejected the priceless citizenship, but also abhor, by word and by silence, the few among them who are genuinely disposed toward us; at every turn they suspect that, with their most infamous way of life, they may swiftly overthrow our affairs.

Therefore, fully persuaded by proofs that these people bear us ill will in every way, and taking forethought lest, if some sudden disturbance should afterward arise against us, we should have these impious people as traitors at our back and barbarous enemies,

we have ordered that as soon as this letter arrives you are at once to send to us those who dwell among you, together with their wives and children, with insults and abuse, confined on all sides in iron bonds, for a death without remedy and infamous, fitting for enemies.
For when these have been punished together, we have concluded that for the remaining time our affairs will be fully established in firm order and the best condition.
Whoever shelters any of the Jews, from the aged down to the infant, even to those at the breast, shall with his whole house be racked to death under the most odious tortures.

Anyone who wishes may inform, on the terms that he shall receive the property of the one who falls under punishment, together with about nineteen pounds of silver{e} from the royal treasury, and shall be crowned with his freedom.
Every place where a sheltered Jew is detected at all shall be made untrodden and burned with fire, and shall be shown wholly useless to every mortal creature for all time."
Such was the form in which the letter was written.

notes.text: Or "a pretext being given by the rumor that they hindered others from keeping the laws"; the Greek is obscure.
Or "they attached no small blame to them."
Coele-Syria ("hollow Syria") is the region between the Lebanon ranges, and more broadly the southern Levant.
Greek "of the priests always," perhaps of the state cults; the sense is uncertain.
Greek "two thousand drachmas"; a drachma was about 0.15 oz (4.3 g), so the total is about 19 lb (8.6 kg).

verses.text: Everywhere this decree arrived, a public feast was set up for the Gentiles with shouting and joy, as the hostility long since hardened in their minds was now being shown forth with boldness.

But among the Jews there was unspeakable mourning and an all-lamenting cry with tears, their hearts set on fire on every side with groans, as they bewailed the destruction unexpectedly and suddenly decreed against them.
What district or city, or what inhabited place at all, or what streets were not filled with wailing and lamentation for them?

For with such bitterness and pitiless soul were they sent off together by the generals in each city that, at the extraordinary punishments, even some of their enemies, setting before their eyes the common pity and reckoning the uncertain overturning of life, wept at their most miserable sending away.

For an old man was led along, crowned with full gray hair, whose feet, bent over from the sluggishness of age, were forced by the impetus of a violent driving to make a swift march, without any respect.

And young women who had just entered the bridal chamber for the partnership of life, receiving laments instead of delight, their myrrh-drenched hair fouled with dust, were led unveiled and together raised a dirge instead of wedding songs, as if torn by the claws of foreign whelps.{a}
Bound, in public view, they were dragged by force as far as the putting on board the ship.

Their husbands, nooses instead of garlands wound about their necks, in the prime of youthful age, spent the remaining days of their marriage festivities in dirges instead of feasting and youthful ease, seeing Hades already lying at their feet.
They were brought down, led like wild beasts under constraint of iron bonds; some were nailed by the neck to the benches of the ships, and some had their feet made fast in unbreakable fetters;
moreover, with the close-set planking laid over above them, so that with their eyes darkened on every side they might receive the treatment of traitors throughout the whole voyage.

When they had been brought to the place called Schedia{b} and the voyage along the coast was completed, as had been decreed by the king, he ordered them to be encamped in the hippodrome before the city, which was of immense circuit and very well suited for making them an example to all who went down into the city and to those from it who set out into the country for travel abroad, so that they might not mingle with his forces nor be counted worthy of any enclosure at all.
When this had been done, he heard that their countrymen from the city were going out in secret and frequently lamenting the inglorious misery of their brothers.
Enraged, he ordered that they too be dealt with carefully in the same way as the others, falling short in no way of their punishment;

and that the whole race be registered by name, not for the hard labor of works briefly indicated before,{c} but that, after being racked with the outrages commanded, they should in the end be blotted out within the time of a single day.
So the registration of these people took place with bitter haste and zealous diligence from the rising of the sun until its setting, coming to no end over forty days.

The king, greatly and continually filled with joy, held banquets before all the idols with a mind far astray from the truth and a profane mouth, praising things dumb and unable to speak to them or help them, while uttering improper words against God.
After the aforesaid interval of time, the scribes reported to the king that they were no longer able to carry out the registration of the Jews because of their immeasurable multitude,
though most were still in the countryside, some still assembled in their houses and some in the place itself, since it was impossible for all the generals in Egypt.{d}
When he threatened them more harshly, as having been bribed to devise their escape, it came about that he was clearly assured on this point,
when they declared with proof that both the papyrus and the writing reeds they used had already given out.
This was the working of the invincible providence of him who was helping the Jews from heaven.

notes.text: Or "foreign cubs"; the image is of animals tearing their prey. The Greek is obscure.
Schedia was a river port on the canal linking Alexandria with the Nile, a short distance southeast of the city.
The Greek of this phrase is obscure; it may refer to the forced labor mentioned in 2:28.
The Greek of this verse is obscure.

verses.text: Then, calling Hermon, who was in charge of the care of the elephants, filled with heavy wrath and bile and wholly unbending,

he commanded him on the coming day to give all the elephants to drink with lavish handfuls of frankincense and much unmixed wine, they being five hundred in number, and, when they had been made savage by the unstinted supply of drink, to lead them in to meet the doom of the Jews.
Giving these orders, he turned to his feasting, gathering those of his Friends and of the army who were most hostile toward the Jews.
And Hermon, the master of the elephants, carried out the order punctiliously.

The attendants assigned to these matters went out toward evening and bound the hands of the wretched people, and contrived the other means of securing them through the night, thinking that the race would meet the end of its destruction all at once.
But the Jews, who seemed to the Gentiles to be bereft of all protection because of the constraint of bonds surrounding them on every side,
all called with tears, with a cry hard to quiet, upon the Lord Almighty, who rules over every power, their merciful God and Father, praying
that he would turn back the unholy design against them and rescue them, with a magnificent manifestation, from the doom lying ready at their feet.
So their entreaty went up fervently to heaven.
Hermon, having watered the merciless elephants until they were filled with the great supply of wine and sated with the frankincense, was at the court at dawn to report about these things to the king.
But the good creation of time, from of old cast upon night and day by him who grants it to all whom he wills, sleep, he sent a portion of to the king;{a}
and by the working of the Master he was held fast in a most sweet and deep sleep, greatly thwarted in his lawless purpose and much deceived in his unbending reckoning.

The Jews, having slipped past the hour that had been signaled beforehand, gave praise to their holy God, and once more they besought the One quick to be reconciled to display before the haughty nations the strength of his mighty hand.
When it was now nearly the middle of the tenth hour,{b} the officer assigned to the invitations, seeing the guests assembled, went and nudged the king.
Rousing him with difficulty, he pointed out that the time of the banquet was already slipping past, giving him an account of these matters.
The king, considering this, turned to his drinking and ordered those who had come to the banquet to recline opposite him.
When this was done, he urged them to give themselves to feasting and, being highly honored, to devote the present part of the banquet to merriment.
As the conversation went on at length, the king called Hermon and asked with bitter threats for what reason the Jews had been allowed to survive the past day.
When Hermon pointed out that he had carried out the order by night, and his Friends bore witness with him,

the king, having a cruelty worse than that of Phalaris,{c} said that they could thank his sleep for this day; "but without delay, for the coming day, get the elephants ready in the same way for the annihilation of the lawless Jews."
When the king had spoken, all who were present gladly agreed together with joy, and each departed to his own house.
And they spent the time of night not so much in sleep as in devising every kind of mockery for those who seemed wretched.
The cock had just crowed at dawn when Hermon, having armed the beasts, was setting them in motion in the great colonnade.
The crowds throughout the city had gathered for the most pitiable spectacle, eagerly waiting for morning.

And the Jews, their breath being drawn out of them for the briefest time,{d} stretching their hands toward heaven in a tearful supplication with mournful strains, begged the greatest God to help them again speedily.
The sun's rays were not yet spreading, and while the king was receiving his Friends, Hermon stood by and summoned him to go out, pointing out that the king's desire lay ready.

Receiving the report and struck with amazement at the lawless going out, being wholly overcome by lack of understanding, he asked what the matter was for which this had been completed for him with such haste.{e}
This was the working of God, who rules over all, who had put into his mind a forgetfulness of what he had previously devised.
Hermon and all the Friends pointed to the beasts and the forces: "They have been made ready, O king, in accordance with your earnest purpose."
But he was filled with heavy bile at these words, because by the providence of God his every thought about these matters had been scattered; and gazing intently at him he said with threats,

"If your parents were present, or your children's offspring, I would have prepared them as this abundant feast for the wild beasts, instead of the Jews, who are blameless toward me and have shown complete and firm loyalty to my ancestors in an outstanding way.
Indeed, were it not for the affection of our upbringing together and your service, you would have been deprived of life instead of them."{f}
Thus Hermon had to endure a threat he never looked for, full of peril; he shrank in his look and countenance.
And the Friends, one by one sullenly slipping away, dismissed those who had gathered, each to his own occupation.
And the Jews, hearing what had come from the king, praised the Lord, the God who manifests himself, the King of kings, since they had obtained this help also from him.
But the king, according to the same customs, set up the whole banquet again and urged the guests to turn to merriment.
And calling Hermon, he said with threats, "How many times must I give you orders about these very things, you most wretched man?
Arm the elephants now once more for tomorrow, for the annihilation of the Jews."
But the kinsmen reclining with him, marveling at his unstable mind, put forward the following:

"O king, how long will you put us to the test in this way, ordering now for the third time that they be destroyed, and again undoing by a change of mind, when it comes to the deed, what you have decided?
Because of this the city is in turmoil through the suspense; and being thronged with mobs it is already in danger of being plundered many times over."

Thereupon the king, a Phalaris in every way, filled with senselessness and counting as nothing the changes of mind that had taken place in him for the protection of the Jews, swore a most futile oath, firmly determining to send them without delay to Hades, mangled by the knees and feet of the beasts,

and that he would march against Judea, swiftly make it level with the ground by fire and spear, and, burning to the ground with fire their temple which was not to be trodden by us, would quickly make it empty forever of those who offer sacrifice there.
Then the Friends and kinsmen departed, overjoyed and confident, and posted the forces at the most suitable places of the city for keeping guard.

And the master of the elephants, having driven the beasts into an almost maddened state, as one may say, with most fragrant drinks of wine mixed with frankincense, and frightfully decked out with gear,
about dawn, when the city was already filled with countless crowds all around the hippodrome, went into the court and urged the king on to the matter at hand.

And he, his impious mind filled with heavy wrath, rushed out with the whole mass of the beasts, wishing with unwounded heart and with the pupils of his eyes to watch the painful and miserable destruction of those already marked out.
When the Jews saw the dust of the elephants going out at the gate and of the armed force following and of the crowd's march, and heard the deep-sounding din,

thinking that this was the last turning point of life for them, the end of their most miserable suspense, they turned to pity and laments and kissed one another, embracing their relatives and falling on their necks, parents on children and mothers on young daughters, while other women held newborn babes at their breasts, drawing their last milk.
Nevertheless, recalling the help that had come to them before from heaven, they flung themselves face down with one accord, and taking the infants from the breasts
they cried out with an exceedingly loud voice, beseeching the Sovereign of all power to have pity on them with a manifestation, now that they stood at the gates of Hades.

notes.text: The Greek of this verse is obscure; the sense is that God sent the king sleep.
About 3:30 in the afternoon, the hours being counted from sunrise.
Phalaris, tyrant of Acragas in Sicily in the sixth century BC, was proverbial for cruelty; he was said to roast his victims in a bronze bull.
Or "through the moment that drew out their souls"; the Greek is obscure.
The Greek of this verse is obscure.
The Greek of vv. 31–32 is obscure, and the sense given is approximate.

verses.text: Then a certain Eleazar, a man of note among the Jews from the countryside, who had already reached old age and was adorned with every virtue throughout his life, restrained the elders around him from calling upon the holy God,{a} and prayed as follows:
"King of great power, Most High, God Almighty, who govern all creation with compassion,
look upon the offspring of Abraham, upon the children of sanctified Jacob, the people of your sanctified portion, perishing unjustly as strangers in a strange land.

Father, you destroyed Pharaoh, once the ruler of this Egypt, who abounded in chariots and was lifted up in lawless boldness and a boastful tongue, drowning him in the sea with his arrogant army, and you made the light of mercy shine on the race of Israel.

Sennacherib, the oppressive king of the Assyrians, exulting in his countless forces, who had already taken the whole earth under his hand by the spear and was raised up against your holy city, speaking oppressive things with pomp and boldness, you, O Master, broke, showing your might plainly to many nations.

The three companions in Babylonia, who willingly gave their lives to the fire so as not to serve empty things, you rescued unharmed to a hair, bedewing the fiery furnace and sending the flame on all their adversaries.{b}
Daniel, hurled down into the ground by the slanders of envy to be food for lions, you led up to the light unharmed.{c}
And Jonah, wasting away in the belly of the deep-bred sea monster, you looked upon, Father, and showed him unharmed to all his household.{d}
And now, you who hate insolence, abounding in mercy, judge of all, appear quickly to those of the race of Israel who are being outraged by abominable, lawless Gentiles.
And if our life has been entangled in ungodliness in our exile, rescue us from the hand of the enemies, and destroy us, O Master, by whatever doom you choose.
Let not the vain-minded bless their vain idols for the destruction of your beloved, saying, 'Not even their God rescued them.'
But you, Eternal One, who have all strength and all dominion, look now; have mercy on us, who by the senseless insolence of lawless men are being removed from life in the manner of traitors.
Let the Gentiles cower today before your invincible power, O honored One, who have power to save the race of Jacob.
The whole multitude of infants and their parents beseech you with tears.

Make it known to all the nations that you stand with us, O Lord, and have not turned your countenance away from us; rather, as you declared, 'Even while they were in their enemies' land, I did not disregard them,'{e} so accomplish it, Lord."
Just as Eleazar was ending his prayer, the king came along by the hippodrome with the beasts and all the haughtiness of his force.
When the Jews saw this, they cried out loudly to heaven, so that the neighboring valleys echoed with them and caused an irrepressible panic in the whole army.

Then the most glorious, almighty, and true God, making his holy face shine forth, opened the gates of heaven, and out of them came down two angels in glory, dreadful to look upon, plain to the sight of everyone except the Jews.
They stood against the force of the adversaries and filled it with confusion and cowardice, and bound them with immovable fetters.
Even the king's body began to shudder, and forgetfulness seized his heavy-tempered boldness.
And the beasts wheeled about against the armed troops coming behind them, trampling and wiping them out.
Then the king's wrath was turned to pity and tears on account of what he had devised before.
For when he heard the outcry and saw them all fallen face down to their destruction, he wept and angrily threatened his Friends, saying,

"You are usurping royal power, and have surpassed tyrants in cruelty; and even me, your benefactor, you are attempting to remove now from rule and from life, secretly devising things not to the advantage of the kingdom.
Who took from their homes those who faithfully held the fortresses of the country for us, and senselessly gathered each of them here?
Who so lawlessly surrounded with outrages those who from the beginning have excelled all nations in goodwill toward us in every way, and who have often accepted the worst of human dangers?
Loose, untie their unjust bonds! Send them away in peace to their homes, asking pardon for what has been done.
Release the sons of the almighty, heavenly, living God, who from our ancestors' time until now has granted unhindered stability with glory to our affairs."
These were the things he said; and they, released in an instant, blessed their holy God and Savior, having just escaped death.

Then the king, having summoned to the city the overseer of revenues, bade him furnish the Jews with wines and the rest of what was suitable for feasting for seven days, deciding that in the very place where they had expected to meet destruction they should celebrate their deliverance with all merriment.

Then those who were formerly reviled and near to Hades, or rather had already set foot in it, instead of a bitter and most lamentable doom held a drinking party of deliverance, and, full of joy, divided up for couches the place prepared for their fall and burial.

Ceasing their all-lamenting strain of dirges, they took up the song of their ancestors, praising God, the Savior of Israel and worker of wonders; and casting away all wailing and shrieking they formed dances as a sign of peaceful merriment.
Likewise the king also, holding a great banquet on account of these things, gave thanks unceasingly and magnificently to heaven for the unexpected deliverance that had come to them.

And those who had earlier assumed that they would be destroyed and become food for birds, and had registered them with joy, groaned as they clothed themselves in shame, their fire-breathing boldness utterly quenched.
And the Jews, as we have said before, having formed the dance just mentioned, spent the time in feasting with joyful thanksgivings and psalms.

And establishing a common ordinance about these things for their whole community of sojourners, for generations, they set the aforementioned days to be kept as days of merriment, not for tippling and greed, but for the salvation brought about for them by God.
They petitioned the king, asking for their release to their homes.

Now they had been registered from the twenty-fifth of Pachon to the fourth of Epiphi (in July–August),{f} for forty days; and their destruction was set from the fifth of Epiphi to the seventh, for three days,
during which the Ruler of all, magnificently manifesting his mercy, rescued them all together unscathed.
They feasted, being supplied with everything by the king, until the fourteenth, the day on which they made their petition for their release.
The king, consenting to them, wrote for them the following letter to the generals in every city, magnanimously expressing his earnest concern:

notes.text: Or "having bidden the elders around him to call upon the holy God"; the Greek can be taken either way.
See Dan 3; Song of the Three 23–27 (Greek Dan 3:46–50).
See Dan 6.
See Jonah 1:17–2:10.
Compare Lev 26:44.

Pachon and Epiphi are the ninth and eleventh months of the Egyptian calendar. In the Ptolemaic civil calendar of about 217 BC the dates given here would fall roughly from early July to mid-August; by the later fixed Alexandrian calendar the dates would fall in May–June. The exact equivalents are uncertain.

verses.text: "King Ptolemy Philopator, to the generals in Egypt and to all who are appointed over affairs: greetings and good health.
We ourselves are in good health, and so are our children, the great God directing our affairs as we choose.
Certain of our Friends, out of malice frequently urging us, won us over to assembling the Jews under our rule into companies and chastising them, as deserters, with outlandish penalties,
alleging that our affairs would never be in good order, because of the ill will these people have toward the other nations, until this was accomplished.

They brought them down in bonds with abuse like slaves, or rather like traitors, and without any inquiry or examination tried to do away with them, having armed themselves with a cruelty more savage than the custom of the Scythians.{a}

But we, threatening them severely for these things, in keeping with the clemency we have toward all people, barely granted them their lives; and having come to know that the God of heaven surely shields the Jews, fighting on their side always as a father for his sons,
and taking into account the firm goodwill of friendship they have toward us and our ancestors, we have justly acquitted them of every charge of whatever kind.
We have also commanded that all return, every man, to his own property, with nobody whatever doing them any hurt or casting up to them what has unreasonably taken place.

Understand that should we contrive some wicked scheme against these people, or vex them in the least, it is no mortal but God Most High, master of every power, whom we shall find set against us, beyond escape, forever, to avenge these deeds. Farewell."

On receiving this letter, they did not hurry at once about their departure, but they requested of the king that those of the race of the Jews who had of their own accord transgressed against the holy God and the law of God should receive through them the punishment they deserved,{b}
alleging that men who for their stomach's sake had broken the commands of God would never be loyal to the commands of the king either.

He, accepting that they spoke the truth and commending them, gave them full license to destroy freely, without any royal authorization or supervision, those who had transgressed the law of God in every place under his kingdom.
Then, applauding him as was fitting, their priests and the whole multitude, shouting "Hallelujah,"{c} departed with joy.
And on the way they put to death any of their countrymen they came upon who had become defiled, and killed them as a public example.
On that day they slew more than three hundred men, and they kept the day as a festival with joy, having subdued the profane.

But they themselves, who had held fast to God to the death and had obtained complete deliverance and release, set out from the city with shouting,{d} giving thanks with praises and melodious hymns to the God of their ancestors, the holy Savior of Israel.
When they had arrived at Ptolemais, called "rose-bearing" because of the character of the place,{e} where the fleet waited for them seven days in accordance with their common resolve,
there they held a drinking feast of deliverance, the king generously supplying them with everything needed for the journey, each one, as far as his own house.
And having landed in peace with fitting thanksgivings, there likewise they resolved to keep these days also as days of merriment for the time of their sojourning.

These they consecrated on a pillar, and having founded a house of prayer where the drinking feast had been held, they went away unhurt, at liberty, exceedingly glad, brought safely through by land and sea and river at the king's command, each to his own home.{f}
And they had greater authority among their enemies than before, with honor and awe, and were not shaken at all by anyone with respect to their possessions.

And all of them recovered all their belongings according to the registry, so that those who held anything gave it back to them with the greatest fear, the great God having done great deeds perfectly for their deliverance.
Blessed be the Deliverer of Israel for all time! Amen.

notes.text: The Scythians, nomads north of the Black Sea, were proverbial among Greeks for savagery.
The Greek of this verse is awkwardly constructed.
Hebrew for "Praise the LORD."
Or "set out from the city of the shouting"; the Greek is obscure.
Ptolemais here is probably a town on the Nile in the Arsinoite district (the Fayum), not the coastal city in Palestine.
The Greek text followed here breaks off after "each to his"; the words "own home" are supplied from the sense, and the opening of v. 21 is likewise incomplete.
